questions.question: A ball is thrown from S at an angle to the horizontal. X, Y and Z are points on its trajectory (Y is the highest point). Which row (A–D) of the table best represents the velocity and acceleration of the ball?
questions.answer: The velocity is tangential (horizontal at Y) and the acceleration is always downwards.

questions.question: Which of the following does **not** affect the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit?
questions.answer: $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ does not depend on the satellite's mass.
options: The mass of the planet it orbits.
The gravitational force of the planet.

questions.question: A car of mass $m$ travels with constant speed $v$ around a circle of radius $r$. It is at the western-most point, as shown. Which statement best describes the net force on the car at this position?
questions.answer: The net force is $mv^2/r$ towards the centre (east here).
options: There is no net force because it is in uniform circular motion.
The net force depends on $v$, $m$ and $r$ and is directed towards the centre.
The net force depends on $v$, $m$ and $r$ and is directed towards the west.
The net force is the sum of the centripetal force and the gravitational force on the car.

questions.question: The speed of an electric motor with no load is limited by the:
questions.answer: The back emf rises with speed until the net current only just overcomes friction.
options: current that can flow through the motor's coils.
back emf produced in the motor.

questions.question: The soft iron core of a transformer is usually laminated. What is the main purpose of this?
questions.answer: Laminations break up the paths for eddy currents, reducing heating losses.
options: To reduce eddy currents in the core.
To increase the permeability of the core.
To reduce the electrical resistance of the core.
To reduce the flux linkage of the two coils.

questions.question: Masses $2M$ (hung at B) and $M$ (hung at C) are on a lever with fulcrum A. When released, mass $M$ accelerates downwards. Given AB $=R_1$ and AC $=R_2$, what can be said about $R_1$ and $R_2$?
questions.answer: $MgR_2>2MgR_1$.

questions.question: A low Earth orbit satellite experiences a gravitational force $F_g$. Its altitude is doubled to reduce orbital decay. What is the new force of gravity on it?
questions.answer: Doubling the *altitude* (not the distance from Earth's centre) changes $r$ only slightly, for example from 6700 km to 7000 km, so $F$ falls by a factor of about $(7000/6700)^2\approx1.1$.

questions.question: Which of these transmutations of uranium-235 currently occurs naturally on Earth?
questions.answer: Spontaneous alpha decay occurs naturally; the others require neutron bombardment.

questions.question: A black body at 4140 K radiates maximum intensity at $7.00\times10^{-7}$ m. If its temperature is increased by 1000 K, at approximately what wavelength is the maximum intensity?
The work function of aluminium is 4.08 eV. What wavelength of light is needed to eject an electron from its surface?
questions.answer: $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{\phi}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^8}{4.08\times1.602\times10^{-19}}$.

questions.question: Two students in windowless railway carriages test Newton's second law. Carriage A moves at a constant velocity of $0.75c$; carriage B is moving at 20 m s$^{-1}$ and slowing down. Which best describes the likely results?
questions.answer: A is an inertial frame; B is accelerating and so is not.
options: Only the experiment in carriage A confirms Newton's second law.
Only the experiment in carriage B confirms Newton's second law.
Neither experiment confirms Newton's second law.
Both experiments confirm Newton's second law.

questions.question: A muon and antimuon, essentially at rest, annihilate to form two gamma photons of total energy $3.38\times10^{-11}$ J. Which is closest to the mass of a single muon?
The Davisson–Germer experiment provided evidence to support:
questions.answer: Electrons were diffracted by a nickel crystal.
options: the accepted value of the charge of the electron.
the particle nature of the electron.
the wave nature of the electron.
the presence of a compact, positive nucleus in the atom.

questions.question: Erwin Schrödinger's main contribution to physics is best described as:
questions.answer: His wave equation gives probability distributions for electrons.
options: postulating that particles can behave as waves.
postulating that waves can behave as particles.
explaining the wavelengths of the lines in the hydrogen emission spectrum.
describing the likelihood of finding an electron in a certain position.

questions.question: The graph shows how average binding energy per nucleon varies with mass number. What can be concluded?
questions.answer: Greater binding energy per nucleon means greater stability.
options: Hydrogen-1 is the most stable nuclide in the Universe.
A nucleus of mass number 50 is more stable than one of mass number 200.
A nucleus of mass number 200 is more stable than one of mass number 50.
Nuclides of mass number below 50 release energy by fission.

questions.question: A transformer has a turns ratio (primary : secondary) of 5 : 2. The primary draws 0.25 A from a 200 V AC supply and the secondary current is 0.50 A. What is the efficiency?
questions.answer: $V_s=80$ V, so efficiency $=\dfrac{80\times0.50}{200\times0.25}=80\%$.

questions.question: P, Q and R are parallel conductors of equal length $L$, as shown. P carries $2I$ and Q carries $I$ in the same direction; R carries $I$ in the opposite direction. P and R are fixed. With $k=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}$, what is the net force on Q?
questions.answer:
P attracts Q (left): $\dfrac{k(2I)(I)L}{2d}=\dfrac{kI^2L}{d}$. R repels Q (also left): $\dfrac{kI^2L}{d}$. Total $\dfrac{2kI^2L}{d}$ to the left.

*Note: the school's key gives C (to the right); the direction is to the left.*

questions.question: A security gate's receiving coil has radius 50 cm and 35 turns, and experiences an induced emf of magnitude 28.5 mV. At what rate must the magnetic flux density inside the coil be changing?
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{NA}=\dfrac{0.0285}{35\times\pi\times0.50^2}$.

*Note: the paper gives the units as Wb s$^{-1}$; a rate of change of flux density has units T s$^{-1}$.*

questions.question: A spacecraft carries a light clock with mirrors 5.00 m apart (proper length) and moves at $0.60c$ relative to the galaxy, along the line AB. One period is the time for light to go from A to B and back. In the galaxy's frame, the period is closest to:

In an indoor soccer match it is a foul if the ball touches the ceiling after a goalkeeper's kick. The ceiling is 10 m high and the keeper always kicks the ball (from ground level) at 20 m s$^{-1}$. What is the maximum angle of the kick so that a foul is not committed?
questions.answer:
At the highest point $v_y=0$ and the height may be at most 10 m:
$$0=(20\sin\theta)^2-2(9.8)(10)\ \Rightarrow\ \sin\theta=\frac{14.0}{20}=0.70$$
$$\theta=44.4^\circ$$

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: A goalkeeper kicks a ball from ground level at 20 m s$^{-1}$ at $44.4^\circ$ to the horizontal. Find the velocity of the ball 2.0 s after it is kicked.
questions.answer:
$v_x=20\cos44.4^\circ=14.3$ m s$^{-1}$

$v_y=20\sin44.4^\circ-9.8\times2.0=-5.6$ m s$^{-1}$

$v=\sqrt{14.3^2+5.6^2}=15.3$ m s$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{5.6}{14.3}\approx21^\circ$ below the horizontal.

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: A car of mass $m$ turns a corner of radius $r$ metres on a flat road. The friction is just enough for it to turn at $v$ km h$^{-1}$. It then meets an oil spill that halves the friction. What is the maximum speed at which the car can now turn without skidding?
questions.answer:
Friction provides the centripetal force: $F_f=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ (with $v$ in consistent units).

With half the friction, $\dfrac{F_f}{2}=\dfrac{mv_{new}^2}{r}$, so $v_{new}^2=\dfrac{v^2}{2}$.

$$v_{new}=\frac{v}{\sqrt2}\approx0.71v\ \text{km h}^{-1}$$

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: A banked curved road has a radius of 50 m and a recommended maximum speed of 40 km h$^{-1}$. With the aid of a labelled force diagram, determine the angle at which the road is banked if the tyres exert no sideways force.
questions.answer:
The only forces are the weight and the normal force; their sum is the horizontal centripetal force (diagram).

$N\cos\theta=mg$ and $N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}$.

With $v=40/3.6=11.1$ m s$^{-1}$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{11.1^2}{50\times9.8}=0.252$, so $\theta=14^\circ$.

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: Planets X and Y move anticlockwise in circular orbits about a star. Their orbital radii are in the ratio 2 : 5. Initially they are aligned in a straight line with the star. Five years later planet X has rotated through 120°, as shown. Determine how long planet Y takes to orbit the star.
questions.answer:
X covers one third of its orbit in 5 years, so $T_X=15$ years.

By Kepler's third law $\dfrac{T_Y^2}{T_X^2}=\dfrac{r_Y^3}{r_X^3}$:
$$T_Y=15\times\left(\tfrac52\right)^{3/2}=59\ \text{years}$$

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: Discuss the importance of Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's third law in understanding and calculating the motion of satellites around Earth.
questions.answer:
**Newton's law** states $F=\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$. It identifies gravity as the force that keeps a satellite in orbit: it acts towards Earth's centre and so provides the centripetal force. This explains *why* satellites orbit, and why gravity weakens with distance.

**Orbital speed.** Equating $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ gives $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$. The speed depends only on the central mass and radius, not on the satellite's mass; lower satellites must move faster.

**Kepler's third law.** Substituting $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ gives
$$\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$$
Kepler found $r^3/T^2$ constant empirically; Newton's law explains the constant. For all Earth satellites the ratio is the same, so the period at any radius can be found, or Earth's mass can be determined from one satellite (such as the Moon).

**Applications.** A geostationary satellite needs $T$ equal to one sidereal day, which gives $r\approx4.2\times10^7$ m (altitude about 36 000 km), above the equator. Low Earth orbit satellites have periods of about 90 minutes, useful for imaging. Launch speeds and orbit transfers are planned with these relationships.

**Limitations.** The equations assume a single spherical central mass and circular (or ideal elliptical) orbits. Real orbits are perturbed by Earth's oblateness, the Moon and Sun, and atmospheric drag, which causes orbital decay; very precise timing (GPS) also needs relativity.

**Judgement:** both are fundamental: Kepler's law describes the pattern, Newton's law explains it and makes it quantitative, and together they allow satellites to be designed and predicted with high accuracy.

*Note: the school file has no solution for this question; this answer was written for this site.*

questions.question: A hand generator contains both a slip-ring commutator and a split-ring commutator, so it can produce AC or DC. Two students each turned it while it was connected to a cathode ray oscilloscope, giving the displays shown. Determine whether each student used the split-ring or the slip-ring commutator. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: Both students used the split-ring commutator. Each trace stays on one side of zero (positive for A, negative for B), so the output never reverses. A split ring swaps the external connections every half turn, at the same moment the emf induced in the coil reverses, giving DC. A slip ring would give a voltage alternating about zero.

questions.question: A hand generator contains both a slip-ring commutator and a split-ring commutator, so it can produce AC or DC. Two students each turned it while it was connected to a cathode ray oscilloscope, giving the displays shown. Account for the differences between the displays for Student A and Student B.
questions.answer:
- **Polarity:** B's output is negative while A's is positive. B turned the handle in the opposite direction (or the magnet polarity or connections were reversed), so the flux changes in the opposite sense and, by Lenz's law, the induced emf is reversed.
- **Size and frequency:** B's pulses are larger and closer together. B turned the generator faster, giving a greater rate of change of flux and so a larger emf ($\varepsilon=-N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$), with more pulses each second.

questions.question:
An experiment measured the lifetime $T$ of a high-speed tau lepton in the laboratory frame as a function of its speed $v$.

| $v$ ($\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$) | $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ | $T$ ($\times10^{-13}$ s) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.00 | 1.06 | 3.08 |
| 1.50 | 1.15 | 3.35 |
| 2.00 | 1.34 | 3.89 |
| 2.50 | ? | 5.25 |
| 2.75 | 2.50 | 7.26 |

Determine the missing value of $\gamma$.

An experiment measured the lifetime $T$ of a high-speed tau lepton in the laboratory frame as a function of its speed $v$.

| $v$ ($\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$) | $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ | $T$ ($\times10^{-13}$ s) |

Draw a graph of $T$ (vertical axis) against $\gamma$.
questions.answer: Plot the five points with labelled axes and scales that fill most of the grid, then draw a straight line of best fit.

questions.question:
An experiment measured the lifetime $T$ of a high-speed tau lepton in the laboratory frame as a function of its speed $v$.

| $v$ ($\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$) | $\gamma=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$ | $T$ ($\times10^{-13}$ s) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.00 | 1.06 | 3.08 |
| 1.50 | 1.15 | 3.35 |
| 2.00 | 1.34 | 3.89 |
| 2.50 | 1.81 | 5.25 |
| 2.75 | 2.50 | 7.26 |

Using a graph of $T$ against $\gamma$, determine the lifetime of the tau lepton in its rest frame.
questions.answer:
Time dilation gives $T=\gamma T_0$, so the gradient of the line of best fit is $T_0$. Using two well separated points on the line, for example $(1.20,\ 3.48)$ and $(2.40,\ 6.96)$ (in $10^{-13}$ s):
$$T_0=\frac{6.96-3.48}{2.40-1.20}\times10^{-13}=2.9\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}$$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Calculate the component of its initial velocity perpendicular to the field.
questions.answer: $v_\perp=8.0\times10^6\sin70^\circ=7.5\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Calculate the component of its initial velocity parallel to the field.
questions.answer: $v_\parallel=8.0\times10^6\cos70^\circ=2.7\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. Outline why the electron moves in a helical path.
questions.answer: The perpendicular velocity component experiences a magnetic force at right angles to it, producing uniform circular motion, while the parallel component experiences no force and stays constant. The combination is a helix.

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. The magnetic flux density is 0.015 T. Calculate the radius of the loops of the helix.
questions.answer: $qv_\perp B=\dfrac{mv_\perp^2}{r}$, so $r=\dfrac{mv_\perp}{qB}=\dfrac{9.109\times10^{-31}\times7.5\times10^6}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.015}=2.8\times10^{-3}$ m

questions.question: An electron travelling at $8.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ enters a uniform magnetic field at $70^\circ$ to the field and moves in a helical path, as shown. The magnetic flux density is 0.015 T. Calculate the distance between adjacent loops of the helix.
questions.answer:
Period of the circular motion: $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}=\dfrac{2\pi\times9.109\times10^{-31}}{1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.015}=2.38\times10^{-9}$ s

Distance advanced in one period: $p=v_\parallel T=8.0\times10^6\cos70^\circ\times2.38\times10^{-9}=6.5\times10^{-3}$ m

*Note: the school gets $6.2\times10^{-3}$ m because it rounded the period down to $2.3\times10^{-9}$ s.*

questions.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to measure the magnetic flux density $B$ of a magnet. A rectangular coil of $N$ turns, width $w$, length $L$ and mass $M$ hangs from one arm of a balance with equal arms, its lower end in a uniform field perpendicular to the plane of the coil. The system is first balanced with no current. When a current $I$ flows, a mass $m$ must be added to the other side to rebalance it. Derive an expression for the magnitude of $B$.
questions.answer:
Only the bottom side (length $w$, $N$ conductors) gives a vertical magnetic force: $F=NBIw$.

The arms are equal (length $\ell$), so the change in torque due to the field is balanced by that of the added weight:
$$NBIw\,\ell=mg\,\ell\ \Rightarrow\ B=\frac{mg}{NIw}$$

questions.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to measure the magnetic flux density $B$ of a magnet. A rectangular coil of $N$ turns, width $w$, length $L$ and mass $M$ hangs from one arm of a balance with equal arms, its lower end in a uniform field perpendicular to the plane of the coil. The system is first balanced with no current. When a current $I$ flows, a mass $m$ must be added to the other side to rebalance it. Why is the expression for $B$ independent of the length $L$ of the coil?
questions.answer: The forces on the two vertical sides are horizontal, equal in size and opposite in direction (their currents flow in opposite directions), so they cancel and produce no change in the balance. Only the horizontal side in the field contributes.

questions.question: Two identical bar magnets hang from identical springs, each with its south pole inside a solenoid. The two solenoids are connected by conducting wires. Magnet A is displaced so that it oscillates vertically, moving into and out of its coil. Magnet B then starts to oscillate, with increasing amplitude. Using physics principles, account for the increase in the amplitude of B's oscillation.
questions.answer:
- As A oscillates, the flux through its solenoid changes continually, so by Faraday's law an alternating emf is induced. By Lenz's law the current opposes A's motion.
- The solenoids form one closed circuit, so the same alternating current flows through B's solenoid.
- This current makes a changing magnetic field that exerts an alternating force on magnet B, at the frequency of A's oscillation.
- The two mass–spring systems are identical, so this driving frequency equals B's natural frequency. Resonance occurs: each push adds energy in phase with B's motion, so its amplitude builds up.
- The energy comes from A (whose oscillation dies down), consistent with conservation of energy.

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. The screen is 3.2 m from the double slit and the slit separation is 0.39 mm. The graph shows the intensity on the screen against distance from its centre. Determine the wavelength of the light.
questions.answer:
Adjacent maxima are about 0.60 cm apart.
$$\lambda=\frac{d\,\Delta x}{L}=\frac{0.39\times10^{-3}\times0.60\times10^{-2}}{3.2}=7.3\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}\ (730\ \text{nm})$$

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. The source is red. It is replaced by a blue source. Predict what (if anything) happens to the separation of the bright fringes. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: The fringes move closer together. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, and the fringe spacing $\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$ is proportional to $\lambda$.

questions.question: A monochromatic source of wavelength $\lambda$, a narrow single slit, a double slit and a screen are arranged as shown, and light and dark bands form on the screen. A polarising filter is placed over each of the two slits, as shown. With the planes of polarisation of the filters parallel, the bands are still seen. When one filter is rotated through 90°, there are no dark bands and the screen is evenly illuminated. Explain why.
questions.answer: Each filter transmits only the component of the electric field oscillating along its own plane of polarisation. With the filters parallel, the waves from the two slits have parallel electric fields, so where they arrive half a wavelength out of step they cancel, giving dark bands. With the filters at 90°, the two electric fields are perpendicular. Perpendicular vibrations cannot cancel each other whatever their phase difference, so there is no destructive (or constructive) interference in intensity: the intensities simply add and the screen is evenly lit.

questions.question: In the 19th and 20th centuries our understanding of the nature of light changed, as debates about its wave and particle nature were challenged by experimental observations. Use this as an example to explain how scientists test and validate models.
questions.answer:
Scientists test a model by deriving predictions from it and comparing them with observation. Agreement supports it; disagreement means it must be refined or replaced.

**Two competing models.** Newton's corpuscle model and Huygens' wave model could both explain reflection and refraction, so these observations could not decide between them. The models made different predictions elsewhere.

**Testing.** Young's double slit experiment produced interference fringes, and diffraction was observed; waves predict these and Newton's particles do not. Foucault found light slower in water, as the wave model predicted. The wave model was accepted, and was strengthened when Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at $c$ and Hertz detected them.

**Anomalies.** Classical wave theory predicted that a black body would emit ever more energy at short wavelengths (the ultraviolet catastrophe), contrary to experiment. Planck matched the data by proposing energy exchanged in quanta, $E=hf$. In the photoelectric effect there is a threshold frequency, emission is immediate and $K_{max}$ depends on frequency not intensity, none of which a wave model predicts.

**New model, new test.** Einstein proposed photons, predicting $K_{max}=hf-\phi$. Millikan's careful measurements confirmed this linear relationship, validating it.

**Refinement.** Interference still needs waves, so neither model was simply discarded: light is described as having wave–particle duality. This shows that models are provisional, are accepted for how well they explain and predict evidence, and are revised when new reproducible observations conflict with them.

questions.question: In 1897 J. J. Thomson measured the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron. With the aid of an annotated diagram, describe how Thomson's experiment can be performed.
questions.answer:
Set up an evacuated discharge tube: a high voltage accelerates cathode rays from the cathode through a slit in the anode, between parallel plates, to a fluorescent screen. Coils outside the tube give a magnetic field at right angles to both the beam and the electric field (diagram).

1. With both fields on, adjust them until the beam is undeflected. The forces balance, $qE=qvB$, so $v=\dfrac{E}{B}$, where $E=V/d$.
2. Switch off the electric field. The beam now follows a circular arc of radius $r$ in the magnetic field alone, with $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Measure $r$ from the deflection.
3. Combine the two:
$$\frac{q}{m}=\frac{v}{Br}=\frac{E}{B^2r}$$

All of $E$, $B$ and $r$ are measurable. Thomson obtained the same large value of $q/m$ with different cathode materials and gases, showing that the particles are a common constituent of atoms.

questions.question: In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed a model of the hydrogen atom. Describe Bohr's model and explain how it accounted for the formation of spectral lines.
Outline TWO shortcomings of Bohr's model of the atom.
questions.answer: First, it works only for hydrogen and other one-electron ions; it cannot predict the spectra of larger atoms. Second, it cannot explain the different intensities of the spectral lines. (Others: it does not explain the splitting of lines in a magnetic field or their fine structure, and it gives no reason why the allowed orbits do not radiate.)

questions.question: Calculate the wavelength of the violet H-delta emission line of hydrogen, produced by a transition from the sixth to the second energy level.
questions.answer:
$$\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{6^2}\right)=1.097\times10^7\times\left(\tfrac14-\tfrac1{36}\right)$$
$$\lambda=4.10\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}\ (410\ \text{nm})$$

questions.question: A carbon-12 atom contains 6 protons and 6 neutrons in its nucleus and has a mass of 12.000 u. Calculate the mass defect of one carbon-12 atom in atomic mass units, assuming the mass of the electrons is negligible.
questions.answer:
Mass of the separate nucleons: $6\times1.673\times10^{-27}+6\times1.675\times10^{-27}=2.0088\times10^{-26}$ kg

Mass of carbon-12: $12.000\times1.661\times10^{-27}=1.9932\times10^{-26}$ kg

$\Delta m=1.56\times10^{-28}$ kg $=\dfrac{1.56\times10^{-28}}{1.661\times10^{-27}}=0.094$ u

questions.question: The graph shows the decay of an unknown radioactive isotope. Use the graph to determine the decay constant of the isotope in s$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
The count rate falls from 850 s$^{-1}$ to 425 s$^{-1}$ in about 3.8 days, so $t_{1/2}=3.8\times86400=3.28\times10^5$ s.
$$\lambda=\frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{3.28\times10^5}=2.1\times10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$$

questions.question: A radioactive isotope is an alpha emitter whose daughter nuclide is polonium-218. Write a nuclear equation for the decay.
